title: Redwood Discovery - Keystone Payments - Latency & Throughput
topics: KV cache and batching impact on throughput
summary: High-level discovery focused on Keystone's latency and throughput SLOs for payment fraud models. Customer currently evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs VPC private option; main concerns are p95 under 300ms for short chat prompts, sustained concurrency 200 with spikes to 700, streaming support, and end-to-end token/sec benchmarking. Next steps: Redwood to share pricing + dedicated sizing worksheet, run a 2-week pilot benchmark, and share SOC2/compliance docs.

transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-04 16:00 PT | Duration: 41m | Attendees: Morgan Lee (Redwood AE), Sanjay Patel (Redwood SE), Emma Clarke (CTO, Keystone), Ravi Shah (Head of ML), Maya Ortiz (Platform Eng), Liam Byrne (SRE)

[00:00] Morgan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Morgan, AE at Redwood. Appreciate you carving out time. Quick round-robin?
[00:07] Emma: Hi all, Emma here, CTO at Keystone. Ravi, Maya and Liam are with me. We're looking at inference options for our fraud models and some chat flows.
[00:15] Morgan: Awesome. Sanjay's the SE, he'll take the deeper latency questions. Sanjay, want to intro?
[00:19] Sanjay: Yep, hi team. Sanjay Patel, Solutions Eng. I work on performance and dedicated/private deployments. Today we'll surface p95 targets, concurrency needs, and run through how Redwood measures tokens per second and streaming.
[00:28] Emma: Cool. So to frame it - our main SLO is p95 end-to-end under 300ms for short prompts (10-50 tokens) for our fraud routing microservice. We also have higher-latency workloads (longer context scoring) where p95 1s is OK. We need sustained concurrency ~200 qps with spikes to 700 for seasonal bursts.
[00:47] Sanjay: Thanks, that's very helpful. When you say end-to-end, do you mean call-to-client, including network and application logic?
[00:53] Ravi: Yes, the full path, including our proxy and some pre/post processing. We can isolate just the infer call if useful.
[00:59] Morgan: Quick clarifying q: are these streaming responses or normal completion calls?
[01:03] Maya: For the fraud microservice, it's single-turn completions - small prompts, single response. For some new chat features, we want streaming for UI snappiness.
[01:12] Sanjay: Ok got it. Two separate profiles: short-turn low latency (10-50 tokens) and streaming chat with longer contexts. For the short-turn, our hosted API can hit p95 sub-200ms in many cases depending on model and region but for sustained 200 concurrency with spikes, Dedicated gives much more predictable throughput.
[01:30] Liam: We need predictability. Our SLA to merchants requires <500ms 95th for decisioning. We can't have noisy neighbors.
[01:37] Sanjay: Understood. Dedicated provides GPU pools you reserve; you get capacity isolation. Private (VPC) adds control plane and network proximity. For the absolute lowest jitter we recommend pinned instances with autoscale policies.
[01:50] Emma: What's the tradeoff on cost vs latency if we move from hosted to dedicated?
[01:55] Sanjay: It depends on utilization. Hosted is op-ex and easier but cost per token higher. Dedicated is committed capacity -- you pay for the pool but cost per token drops at scale; also you get predictable p95 because you avoid neighbor interference. We have a Optimize guide that shows batching/kv cache config impacts.
[02:12] Ravi: Can you explain KV cache and how that affects tokens/sec? A lot of our scoring uses prefix tokens repeated across requests.
[02:18] Sanjay: Sure. Our KV cache stores key/value states for autoregressive decoding; for repeated prefixes we can skip re-computing attention which reduces per-token compute. That increases effective tokens/sec and lowers latency for subsequent requests in a session. For stateless short prompts it'll help if you have repeated context. It does complicate batching a bit.
[02:33] Emma: Do you have numbers for tokens/sec on the models we looked at in the deck? We were comparing an open 7B vs a quantized 13B.
[02:40] Sanjay: Off memory - on A100-ish hardware, for a well-optimized 7B you might see ~1200-1500 tokens/sec single-stream; quantized 13B varies a lot, but with int8 it could be 700-900 tokens/sec. On our newest runtime on H100/RTX-grade we can push higher. These are ballpark, and we'll provide a benchmark sheet.
[02:58] Morgan: Important to call out model selection affects latency more than network in many cases.
[03:03] Ravi: For our use case short prompts are dominant; so 7B or quantized 13B sound fine if p95 < 300ms.
[03:09] Sanjay: Right. Also model seq length matters: if you're using longer context for chat, kv cache helps, but per-token time rises with longer window.
[03:17] Maya: Regarding streaming, what's the overhead to enable streaming? Are there special endpoints?
[03:22] Sanjay: We support streaming via chunked transfer / SSE depending on client. The overhead is minimal; you want to tune chunk sizes and have client-side buffering. Network RTT still matters for first-byte. For short responses streaming may not help p95 because you still pay first-token cost. For interactive chat it improves perceived latency.
[03:37] Liam: Our network egress and VPC peering introduces ~10-20ms. We need to account for that.
[03:42] Sanjay: Yes, and with Private VPC deployments you can colocate inference near your VPC to shave that. We'll document recommendations for region selection and peering.
[03:51] Emma: Can Redwood do token/sec benchmarking with our exact payloads?
[03:55] Morgan: Yes. Typical flow is you provide sample payloads and concurrency profiles, we spin up a dedicated trial pool and run load tests. Sanjay's team will share a checklist.
[04:05] Ravi: We also need to validate p95 across cold start scenarios, and also check how autoscale behaves during spike events.
[04:11] Sanjay: We'll include cold-start tests. Our autoscale can be configured with warm pools and burst capacity to handle spikes; we can simulate traffic patterns you shared and measure time to stabilize and p95 during ramp.
[04:24] Emma: Security wise, we need SOC 2, SSO/SAML, RBAC, and KMS integration; plus data retention controls.
[04:31] Morgan: We will share SOC2 and security docs; Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and audit logs.
[04:38] Maya: One more: do you have recommendations on batch sizing? We want to avoid latency tail increases from over-batching.
[04:44] Sanjay: Yes. We typically suggest small batch thresholds for low-latency paths and larger batches for high throughput offline scoring. Adaptive batching and deadline-based batching helps: small batches trigger off latency SLOs, larger batches if you can accept higher p95. Our Optimize tool can recommend settings based on trace data.
[04:59] Emma: For benchmarking, we care about 95th, 99th, and also p50 for debugging.
[05:05] Sanjay: We'll capture p50/p95/p99 and token/sec histograms. We'll also provide CSV of per-request latency and token counts.
[05:13] Liam: Is there a simple way to compare hosted vs dedicated cost for our projected 1M tokens/day and concurrency profile?
[05:19] Morgan: We'll include a cost model worksheet. For 1M tokens/day and sustained concurrency profile, dedicated often wins if utilization > ~30-40% of committed capacity. We'll show break-even points.
[05:31] Emma: Who's the contact to run the pilot?
[05:33] Morgan: I'll own the pilot engagement + coordination, Sanjay will run the technical tests.
[05:38] Ravi: We'll send sample payloads and a token distribution CSV by Friday.
[05:42] Maya: I'll confirm VPC network constraints and peering options next week.
[05:46] Morgan: Great. Anything else?
[05:48] Emma: One last item - latency SLOs for payments decisioning are strict; we may need a hybrid where sensitive data stays in VPC/private but non-sensitive chat can use hosted. Thoughts?
[05:57] Sanjay: That's a common pattern. We can set routing policies: sensitive traffic to private nodes, general traffic to hosted. Automatic fallback works if private capacity is exhausted. We'll include routing examples.
[06:10] Morgan: Ok let's recap next steps. Sanjay will share benchmark checklist and load test prompts; I'll send pricing and sizing worksheet; Keystone to send payloads; we'll schedule pilot kickoff.
[06:22] Emma: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to seeing the benchmark plan.
[06:26] Morgan: Thanks, we'll follow up with calendar invite for pilot kickoff.
[06:30] End meeting.

Notes/imperfections: occasional transcription mislabels (Sanjay sometimes appears as Speaker 2), product names sometimes transcribed (KV cache -> KV cash), VPC spoken as "V P C".

Links referenced: Redwood dedicated sizing worksheet (link shared after call), benchmark checklist (to be shared), SOC2 + security pack (link to security docs).

Recap: Redwood to run dedicated pilot, provide benchmark artifacts and pricing. Customer to provide payloads and network constraints.
